description: We’re 3rd-year Software Engineering students from Sakarya University, Türkiye, who love turning real-world problems into working software. Our skills: backend (C#/.NET, Java/Spring Boot), mobile (Flutter), databases and data processing. We’re excited to build something meaningful with NASA’s open data in 48 hours.
summary: MarsPath is a web-based EVA route planner for future astronauts on Mars. Using real USGS HiRISE elevation data of Jezero Crater, it computes slope and roughness for a 2×2 km area, finds the safest walking route with A* pathfinding, and checks it against a spacesuit time budget. In our demo mission, the safest route is only 70 m longer than the shortest one but keeps the maximum slope at 6.4° instead of 15.9°, with an estimated 86 minutes of a 192-minute EVA limit. It also ranks reachable science stops, shows real Perseverance Mastcam-Z images and historical MEDA weather, and works on mobile. This matters because safe, data-driven route planning lets astronauts spend less time and risk walking and more time on science.
details:
What it does

MarsPath helps plan a walking EVA on real Martian terrain. The user places a habitat and a target on a HiRISE map of Jezero Crater. MarsPath computes three routes (safest, shortest, balanced), recommends the safest one, and checks whether the full EVA (out + research + back) fits within the time limit.

How it works

1. Data: USGS Mars 2020 TRN HiRISE DTM and orthomosaic, cropped to a 2,000 × 2,000 m area and resampled to a 400 × 400 grid of 5 m cells.

2. Terrain analysis: a Python pipeline computes slope and a normalized roughness value for each cell (max slope 20.2°, 81% of cells below 5°).

3. Routing: 8-neighbour A* search with cost = distance × (α + β·slope + γ·roughness). Cells above a user-adjustable slope limit are impassable.

4. EVA check: walking time from Tobler's hiking function scaled by 0.6 for a suited astronaut; 240-minute EVA with a 20% safety margin and 30 minutes of research time.

Key features

- "Where can we go?": ranks reachable science stops by safety and time margin.

- Adjustable slope limit and route weights; routes update instantly (Web Workers).

- Science stop cards with real Perseverance Mastcam-Z images (sol and image ID shown, labelled "Not taken at this map location").

- Historical MEDA surface conditions (pressure, humidity, sensor temperature, wind) from six sols.

- Elevation profile comparing routes.

- NASA Mars Trek regional context map and the Perseverance landing site as a reference marker.

- Responsive layout for mobile.

Benefits

Planners and crews can compare routes and stops before an EVA using real data, reducing exposure to steep and rough terrain and making better use of limited EVA time.

Tools and technologies

React, TypeScript, Vite, OpenLayers, Recharts, Web Workers, Vitest, Oxlint; Python (NumPy, rasterio, Pillow) for the data pipeline; deployed on Vercel (mirror on Netlify).

Limitations and honesty

This is a preliminary route assessment for planning, not an operational EVA verdict. The area is limited to 2 × 2 km. MEDA data is historical, not a forecast. Scenario values are labelled in the app. The landing site position is approximate.

Next steps

Add a geologic map layer (USGS SIM 3464), cover larger areas and add more science targets.

Use of AI

Frontend code was developed with Claude Code (Anthropic) and the data pipeline and routing code with OpenAI Codex. AI assistants also helped draft documentation and these submission texts. The team logo was created with an AI image tool and is marked "AI-generated" wherever it appears. All code was reviewed, tested (Vitest and Python tests) and validated by the team. All maps, terrain data and rover photos are real NASA/USGS data, not AI-generated.
